## What This Course Is

- This is not a course *about* research. It is a course where **you do research**, start to finish
- You will ask your own question of real data and defend an answer
- By December you will have written and published a **White Paper**
- No prior coding is required, and no math beyond arithmetic and careful reading
- We go slowly and in order, and every assignment feeds the final paper

## What You Will Build

::: {.define}
**Content analysis:** the systematic study of messages; in its quantitative form, the one this course uses, you sort each message into categories by written rules so the results can be counted. Example: marking each chat message as aimed at the streamer, at another viewer, or at the whole room, then counting each kind.
:::

- **Phase one is qualitative:** you read real messages closely until you can say what is there
- **Phase two is quantitative:** you count what you found and test relationships in R

## Four Words You Will Use All Term

::: {.define}
**Variable:** something about a case that can change from one case to the next, where a case is one thing you study, such as one chat message. Example: the `game` column says Fortnite for one stream and Just Chatting for another.
:::

::: {.define}
**Sample:** the smaller set of cases you actually look at. Example: a few thousand messages drawn from the week's 21,964,296.
:::

## Four Words You Will Use All Term (cont.)

::: {.define}
**Codebook:** the document of rules for coding: each variable, its definition, its categories, the decision rules, and examples. Example: the rule that a message tagging the streamer is coded "directed at the streamer."
:::

::: {.define}
**Coding sheet:** the grid where you record the codes, with one row for each thing you code and one column for each variable in the codebook. Example: a spreadsheet with one row per chat message and a column where each message's target is entered.
:::

## How the Two Phases Connect

- Phase one ends in the memo that becomes your codebook; phase two applies it to a sample, then re-codes a share later to show your coding held steady
- Every assignment this term is one piece of that study, in the order you need it

## The Road From Curiosity to Claim

Nothing here is a detour. Each row hands the next one its materials.

## The Shared Example Dataset

[One week of Twitch, November 2018]{.eyebrow}

- **21,964,296 chat messages** across 1,695 channels
- **590,876 stream snapshots**: who was streaming what, to how many people
- The data is real, messy, and public, the kind you would meet in the field
- Bob Ross averaged 3,178 concurrent viewers that week, and xQc averaged 17,363
- This dataset is the shared example the whole class works from
    - Your own study uses whatever source your question needs

## What a Snapshot Is

::: {.define}
**Snapshot:** one record of one stream at one moment, taken about once a minute: its channel, title, game, viewer count, and time. Example: xQc streaming Just Chatting to 19,381 viewers at one moment on November 18, 2018.
:::

## Exercise: Name a Curiosity {.discuss}

Answer each in writing:

- Name one thing about online media you have genuinely wondered about
- Write it as a curiosity, not a research question. "I wonder whether" is enough
- Name what you would need to *observe* to say something defensible about it

You choose a topic in Week 6, and these notes are your starting list.

## The Four Tools

::: {.define}
**R:** a free language and environment for statistical computing and graphics. Example: R counts how many messages each channel posted that week.
:::

::: {.define}
**VS Code:** a free code editor from Microsoft, where you write code and prose in one place. Example: your White Paper's text and its R code open side by side in one window.
:::

None of these tools costs money. Setup walkthroughs are on the course site.

## The Four Tools, Continued

::: {.define}
**Quarto:** an open-source publishing system that turns one file of text and code into a finished website, PDF, or paper. Example: your White Paper is a single Quarto file.
:::

::: {.define}
**Git:** a program that tracks every change to the files in a project, so you can see or return to any earlier version. **GitHub:** a website that hosts those Git projects online. Example: your project's full history sits on GitHub, one dated change at a time.
:::

## What R Looks Like

This is a full analysis, start to finish:

```r
library(v2v)
chat <- twitch_chat()

chat %>%
  group_by(channel) %>%
  summarize(messages = n()) %>%
  arrange(desc(messages))
```

Read it out loud: take the chat data, group it by channel, count the messages, and sort from
most to least. **Code is instructions in order, and that is all it is.**

## What Quarto Gives You

::: {.define}
**Render:** telling Quarto to run the code in your document and build the finished file from it. Example: change the data, render again, and every number in your paper updates.
:::

- One document holds your writing, your code, and your results together
- You never paste a chart into a document and hope it is still current
- The same source can become a website, a Word file, or a PDF
- Your White Paper will be a Quarto document

## Why Version Control Matters

- Git keeps a **time-stamped history** of every change you make
- If you break something, you can go back to when it worked
- GitHub puts that history online, which is where your paper will live
- It is also how you show your work, because a reviewer can retrace every step

::: {.define}
**Reproducibility:** getting the same results again from the same data, the same code, and the same steps. Example: anyone who renders your file on the example data gets your exact message counts.
:::

## The Rules on Using AI

- AI tools are **permitted as a supervised aid**, and you must disclose their use
- Log every use in the **AI-use log** and submit it with each assignment: the tool, what you used it for, and how you **checked its output**
- You are responsible for every claim and every line of code you submit
- The course workspace tells GitHub Copilot to remind you to log each exchange. The reminder does not replace the log
- Using it to avoid learning R will show in the Analyst weeks, when the code gets harder
- Code the AURA Lab R Companion's menus write is not AI. Keep the comment it adds, and you answer for that line like any other
- Ask me if you are unsure whether a use is appropriate
